items.title: 12.9 Stability of the oxidation states of sulfur

source_refs.note: Topic 12.9 with Figure 12.9, printed pages 281-282. The original's Frost curves are schematic.

blocks.text: The stability of the oxidation states of sulfur is explained by a Frost diagram, a plot of nE standard against oxidation state n for the redox couple X(n)/X(0) (Figure 12.9). It shows the relative stabilities of the oxidation states at two extreme pH values, pH 0 and pH 14 (acidic and basic conditions). It can also be regarded as a plot of the standard reaction Gibbs free energy against oxidation state, because -delta G standard = nFE standard, or -delta G standard / F = nE standard, where E standard is the standard reduction potential, F the Faraday constant and n the number of electrons transferred. The more stable oxidation state has the lower nE value (more negative Gibbs energy), so it lies at the lowest position in the diagram; a couple with a more positive slope is a good oxidising agent, and one with a more negative slope a good reducing agent.

blocks.alt: Frost diagram: nE° (V) from −5 to 2 on the vertical axis against oxidation state (n) −II, 0, II, IV, VI. Black dotted line, acidic solution: H2S(g) at about −0.35, S8 at 0, SO2(aq) at about 1.8 and SO4 2− at about 2.25. Blue dotted line, basic solution: S2− at about 0.8, S8 at 0, SO3 2− at about −2.6 and SO4 2− at about −4.6.
blocks.caption: Figure 12.9: Frost diagram for oxidation states of sulfur (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 12.9).

blocks.text: In the diagram for sulfur, +6 (sulfate) is the most thermodynamically stable oxidation state, completely non-oxidising under extremely basic conditions, while under extremely acidic conditions it is very unstable. In basic environments the oxidised sulfur states are all more stable than the elemental form, but under acidic conditions all the oxidised states are less stable than the element.
